content: Ampicillin for Injection, USP is specifically indicated for the treatment of infections caused by susceptible strains of designated organisms under the following conditions: 1. Respiratory Tract Infections: Ampicillin is effective against infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (formerly Diplococcus pneumoniae), Staphylococcus aureus (both penicillinase-producing and non-penicillinase-producing strains), Haemophilus influenzae, and Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. 2. Bacterial Meningitis: Ampicillin is indicated for meningitis caused by Escherichia coli, Group B streptococci, and other Gram-negative bacteria such as Listeria monocytogenes and Neisseria meningitidis. The addition of an aminoglycoside to ampicillin therapy may enhance its effectiveness against Gram-negative bacteria. 3. Gram-negative Sepsis: Ampicillin is effective in treating sepsis caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Salmonella species. 4. Endocarditis: Infections of the heart lining caused by enterococcal strains typically respond to intravenous ampicillin therapy. The addition of an aminoglycoside may improve the efficacy of ampicillin in treating streptococcal endocarditis. 5. Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs): Ampicillin is effective against UTIs caused by susceptible strains of Escherichia coli and Proteus mirabilis. Infections caused by Shigella species (dysentery) also generally respond to oral or intravenous ampicillin therapy. Bacteriological studies should be conducted to identify the causative organisms and determine their susceptibility to ampicillin. However, therapy may be initiated before the results of susceptibility testing are available. The parenteral form of ampicillin should be reserved for moderately severe to severe infections or for patients unable to take oral formulations. Transition to oral ampicillin should be made as soon as it is clinically appropriate. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and preserve the effectiveness of Ampicillin for Injection, USP and other antibacterial drugs, this medication should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy decisions. When necessary, appropriate surgical procedures should be performed in conjunction with antibiotic therapy.
